related_questions.question: What are five causes of asthma?

text_blocks.snippet: While the exact cause of asthma isn't fully understood, several factors contribute to its development. Five common causes or triggers include: allergies, respiratory infections, environmental irritants like smoke and pollution, occupational exposures, and genetics.
snippet_highlighted_words: allergies, respiratory infections, environmental irritants like smoke and pollution, occupational exposures, and genetics

list.title: Allergies:
list.snippet: Exposure to allergens like pollen, dust mites, pet dander, and mold can trigger asthma symptoms.

list.title: Respiratory Infections:
list.snippet: Viral infections like colds and the flu can inflame the airways and worsen asthma.

list.title: Environmental Irritants:
list.snippet: Air pollution, smoke (including secondhand smoke), and strong chemical fumes can irritate the airways and trigger asthma.

list.title: Occupational Exposures:
list.snippet: Certain jobs expose individuals to substances like dust, chemicals, or fumes that can irritate the lungs and cause asthma.

list.title: Genetics:
list.snippet: A family history of asthma, allergies, or eczema increases the likelihood of developing asthma, according to the American Lung Association.

related_questions.question: Does asthma get worse with age?

text_blocks.snippet: Yes, asthma can get worse with age, although it's not a universal rule. While some people with childhood asthma may experience remission, others may find their asthma symptoms worsen as they age, and some adults develop asthma for the first time later in life.
snippet_highlighted_words: Yes, asthma can get worse with age

text_blocks.snippet: Here's why asthma might worsen with age:

list.title: Age-related changes in the lungs:
list.snippet: Lungs naturally become less elastic and chest muscles weaken with age, making it harder to breathe deeply and exhale fully, which can exacerbate asthma symptoms.

list.title: Reduced immune function:
list.snippet: The immune system tends to weaken with age, making older adults more susceptible to respiratory infections (like colds and flu) that can trigger asthma attacks.

list.title: Lifestyle factors:
list.snippet: Older adults may become less active and gain weight, which can also contribute to worsening asthma.

list.title: Comorbidities:
list.snippet: Older adults are more likely to have other health conditions (like heart disease) that can complicate asthma management.

list.title: Treatment challenges:
list.snippet: Arthritis and other age-related issues can make it harder to use inhalers correctly, impacting asthma control.
It's important to note that some individuals develop asthma for the first time as adults, a condition known as adult-onset asthma.
Adult-onset asthma may be more severe and harder to control than childhood-onset asthma, according to some studies, according to the National Institutes of Health (NIH).
Factors like hormonal changes (particularly in women), exposure to allergens and irritants, and being overweight can contribute to adult-onset asthma.
Asthma symptoms can change throughout a person's life, and what was once a mild case can become more severe.
Even if asthma symptoms disappear for a time, they can return later in life.
If you have concerns about your asthma, it's crucial to consult with a healthcare professional for proper diagnosis and management.
